slides.title: Assess the patient before expanding the antibiotic regimen
slides.section: Assess the patient before expanding the antibiotic regimen
paragraphs: A 67-year-old develops a temperature of 38.6 C on hospital day 6 while receiving antibiotics for an abdominal infection. Blood pressure and oxygen requirements are unchanged. A drain and urinary catheter remain in place.
Discuss before reading on. Which findings would require immediate treatment? What would you review before changing antibiotics?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Assess the patient before expanding the antibiotic regimen A 67-year-old develops a temperature of 38.6 C on hospital day 6 while receiving antibiotics for an abdominal infection. Blood pressure and oxygen requirements are unchanged. A drain and urinary catheter remain in place. Discuss before reading on. Which findings would require immediate treatment? What would you review before changing antibiotics? Confirm the temperature and measurement method. Assess blood pressure, oxygenation, mental status, perfusion, and urine output. Reconstruct the timeline of symptoms, procedures, devices, medications, and prior cultures. This module addresses new or persistent inpatient fever, not the full evaluation of prolonged FUO. [1]

slides.title: The urgency depends on sepsis probability and organ dysfunction
slides.section: The urgency depends on sepsis probability and organ dysfunction
rows: Possible septic shock or probable/definite sepsis
Next action
Begin appropriate antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 hour of recognition, while resuscitating and evaluating the source.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
The urgency depends on sepsis probability and organ dysfunction Antibiotic timing follows the 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidance. Clinical assessment Next action Possible septic shock or probable/definite sepsis Begin appropriate antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 hour of recognition, while resuscitating and evaluating the source. Possible sepsis without shock Conduct a rapid, time-limited evaluation. If concern for infection persists, administer antimicrobials within 3 hours of first suspecting sepsis. Low likelihood of infection and no shock Close observation with reassessment can be appropriate. A temperature elevation alone does not require broader antibiotics. Collect indicated cultures before antibiotics if this will not materially delay treatment. Do not wait for a procalcitonin result to treat probable sepsis. [2] Neutropenic fever requires its own urgent empiric treatment pathway. Profound immunosuppression, suspected meningitis, and other time-sensitive syndromes need immediate senior assessment; routine ward observation rules do not apply. [3]

slides.title: Use the history and examination to choose tests
slides.section: Use the history and examination to choose tests
rows: Bacteremia or a central-line source is plausible
Focused evaluation
Obtain blood cultures; use paired peripheral and line samples when evaluating a catheter source. Document collection sites.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Use the history and examination to choose tests Avoid a standing order to culture every body site with each temperature spike. Finding or concern Focused evaluation Bacteremia or a central-line source is plausible Obtain blood cultures; use paired peripheral and line samples when evaluating a catheter source. Document collection sites. New cough, hypoxemia, or respiratory findings Chest imaging; respiratory testing guided by the syndrome and exposures. ICU guidance recommends a chest radiograph for new fever. Urinary findings or unexplained sepsis Evaluate for UTI in context. A catheter or pyuria alone does not establish a urinary source. New unexplained diarrhea Consider C. difficile testing when there are at least 3 unformed stools in 24 hours and no better explanation, such as laxatives. Abdominal pain, ileus, abnormal drainage, or recent surgery Examine the abdomen and wound, review source control, and discuss targeted imaging with the procedural team. [1] [5] For suspected intra-abdominal abscess in a nonpregnant adult, CT is the preferred initial modality in the 2024 IDSA update. Contrast use depends on the clinical question and patient factors. [4] Testing formed stool or repeating a C. difficile test to document cure is not appropriate. [5]

slides.title: Persistent fever can reflect a new source or a noninfectious process
slides.section: Persistent fever can reflect a new source or a noninfectious process
rows: Uncontrolled or newly acquired infection
Question to ask at the bedside
Is a collection undrained, a device infected, or a new syndrome developing?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Persistent fever can reflect a new source or a noninfectious process A differential should lead to a specific reassessment, not an indiscriminate panel. Possibility Question to ask at the bedside Uncontrolled or newly acquired infection Is a collection undrained, a device infected, or a new syndrome developing? Medication reaction Did fever begin after a new drug? Is there rash, eosinophilia, or organ injury? Their absence does not exclude drug fever. Thrombosis or pulmonary embolism Are there compatible symptoms or signs that justify directed testing? Postoperative inflammation or tissue injury Does the course fit the procedure, and is the patient improving? Do not use postoperative timing alone to exclude infection. Transfusion reaction or other inflammatory disease Does the timing or a new examination finding point away from infection? [1] [6] Review the entire medication administration record, including new non-antibiotics. Drug fever is an exclusion diagnosis; rash with organ injury needs evaluation for a serious drug reaction. [1] [6]

slides.title: Persistent fever can reflect a new source or a noninfectious process
slides.section: Persistent fever can reflect a new source or a noninfectious process
rows: Postoperative inflammation or tissue injury
Question to ask at the bedside
Does the course fit the procedure, and is the patient improving? Do not use postoperative timing alone to exclude infection.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Persistent fever can reflect a new source or a noninfectious process A differential should lead to a specific reassessment, not an indiscriminate panel. Possibility Question to ask at the bedside Uncontrolled or newly acquired infection Is a collection undrained, a device infected, or a new syndrome developing? Medication reaction Did fever begin after a new drug? Is there rash, eosinophilia, or organ injury? Their absence does not exclude drug fever. Thrombosis or pulmonary embolism Are there compatible symptoms or signs that justify directed testing? Postoperative inflammation or tissue injury Does the course fit the procedure, and is the patient improving? Do not use postoperative timing alone to exclude infection. Transfusion reaction or other inflammatory disease Does the timing or a new examination finding point away from infection? [1] [6] Review the entire medication administration record, including new non-antibiotics. Drug fever is an exclusion diagnosis; rash with organ injury needs evaluation for a serious drug reaction. [1] [6]

slides.title: Reassessment should produce a specific plan
slides.section: Reassessment should produce a specific plan
paragraphs: For the opening case, review the original diagnosis, cultures, antibiotic activity and dosing, drain output, and most recent imaging. If an abdominal source remains plausible, reassess drainage with surgery or interventional radiology. A broader drug does not replace drainage of an infected collection. [2] [4]

If the patient deteriorates or a new syndrome emerges, treat accordingly. If improving and no new evidence supports infection, avoid broadening solely for persistent fever; reassess whether current antibiotics remain indicated. [2]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Reassessment should produce a specific plan For the opening case, review the original diagnosis, cultures, antibiotic activity and dosing, drain output, and most recent imaging. If an abdominal source remains plausible, reassess drainage with surgery or interventional radiology. A broader drug does not replace drainage of an infected collection. [2] [4] If the patient deteriorates or a new syndrome emerges, treat accordingly. If improving and no new evidence supports infection, avoid broadening solely for persistent fever; reassess whether current antibiotics remain indicated. [2] Example handoff. "New fever without current hemodynamic or respiratory deterioration. Reviewing the abdominal source and drain with the procedural team. Reassess immediately for hypotension, increased oxygen need, or altered mentation."

slides.title: Know which recommendations come from ICU evidence
slides.section: Know which recommendations come from ICU evidence
paragraphs: The 2023 SCCM/IDSA guideline concerns new fever in adult ICU patients without severe immunocompromise. Many recommendations are conditional or best-practice statements. The ward approach here is a clinical adaptation; routine ICU testing should not become a universal ward order set. [1]

When fever remains unexplained, repeat the history and examination before pursuing advanced imaging or broad serologies. The guideline conditionally suggests FDG-PET/CT in selected critically ill patients after unrevealing investigations when transport is acceptable. This is not a first-line test for an isolated ward fever. [1]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Know which recommendations come from ICU evidence The 2023 SCCM/IDSA guideline concerns new fever in adult ICU patients without severe immunocompromise. Many recommendations are conditional or best-practice statements. The ward approach here is a clinical adaptation; routine ICU testing should not become a universal ward order set. [1] When fever remains unexplained, repeat the history and examination before pursuing advanced imaging or broad serologies. The guideline conditionally suggests FDG-PET/CT in selected critically ill patients after unrevealing investigations when transport is acceptable. This is not a first-line test for an isolated ward fever. [1] Discussion variation. The temperature is unchanged, but the patient now has hypotension and confusion. Explain how the urgency changes even before the source is known. [2]
